newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to allow simultaneous local, foreign shares.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to allow simultaneous local, foreign shares.

text.p: Taiwan's Securities and Futures Commission said on Tuesday it was lifting a restriction that has prevented companies from listing shares simultaneously in the Taiwan stock exchange and foreign bourses.
The liberalisation, effective from July 2, applies to local Taiwan companies as well as foreign firms, an official at the regulatory commission told Reuters by telephone.
"From tomorrow onward, Taiwan firms with local listings can list shares in overseas exchanges," the official said. "Likewise, shares of foreign companies can be listed and traded here as well."

The liberalisation not only frees listed Taiwan companies tap capital in foreign markets through overseas rights issues, but also opens the door to speculation on price spreads between shares listed on multiple exchanges, the official said.
The reform aimed to promote stock trading across exchanges to better integrate Taiwan's once-isolated exchange into the international financial system, officials said.

The securities commission official said the liberalisation applied to most major overseas exchanges, including the New York, Nasdaq and Amex in the United States as well as the main exchanges in London, Frankfurt, Tokyo, Osaka, Paris, Amsterdam, Singapore, Sydney, Kuala Lumpur and Bangkok.
Exchanges in arch rival communist China, including the Hong Kong stock exchange, are not included, officials said.
Until now, Taiwan firms listed in Taiwan have been barred from listing shares simultaneously on overseas exchanges.
Since 1992, overseas firms with shares listed in overseas markets have been allowed to tap into Taiwan's share market only through issuance of Taiwan depositary receipts. None has done so to date.

On the other hand, Taiwan firms have been active in listing shares in overseas markets, chiefly through global depositary receipts or American depositary receipts, as well as through primary listings by overseas-registered subsidiaries.
Detailed regulations were being issued by the Securities and Futures Commission.
